### What
Fixes `S_BFM_B32` and `V_BFM_B32` lowering when the masked width and offset add to more than 32. Construct the low-bit mask at offset zero and shift in 32-bit arithmetic so overflow bits are discarded. Width/offset masking, vector EXEC masking and scalar SCC preservation remain intact. For width 2 and offset 31, the expected result is `0x80000000`.

Semantics: [AMD RDNA 1.0 ISA](https://www.amd.com/content/dam/amd/en/documents/radeon-tech-docs/instruction-set-architectures/rdna-shader-instruction-set-architecture.pdf), section 12.1 opcode 36 and section 12.12 opcode 867; [SPIR-V OpBitFieldInsert](https://registry.khronos.org/SPIR-V/specs/unified1/SPIRV.html#OpBitFieldInsert).

The GPU regression uses zero-stride byte buffers with `OOB_SELECT=3`, the raw bounds mode in RDNA ISA section 8.1, Table 35. The earlier fixture selected structured bounds with stride zero and dropped stores when run against current main. The descriptor is corrected; all result and SCC assertions remain, with actual/expected values added to failure messages. The technical-debt entry is placed with related shader entries to avoid shared insertion conflicts.

Windows 11, WinLibs MinGW-w64 GCC 15.2.0 UCRT/POSIX/SEH, Ninja Release, `BUILD_TESTING=ON`, `ANYPS5_ENABLE_SPIRV_TOOLS=ON`; updated to main `d70b89989473ba1f6ae13e44e079e67f1f8a44b0`.

body:
### What

`ComputeThickLayout` sizes the mips of a linear 3D texture from `mip.width` and `mip.height`, which round down (`max(dim >> level, 1)`). Its tiled modes, and the 2D linear path in `ComputeLinearMipLayout`, use the rounded-up element extent (`ShiftCeil`). addrlib rounds up for linear as well: its linear mip loop calls `GetMipSize` (`gfx10addrlib.cpp` L5090), which is `ShiftCeil(Max(mip0Width, 1u), mipId)` (`gfx10addrlib.h` L376-377).

For any level that halves an odd size, the row count, mip offsets and slice size therefore come out smaller than the guest's. Linear 8 bpp 100×60×8 with 4 levels:

| | slice size | surface | mip 0 | mip 1 | mip 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| addrlib | 28,928 | 231,424 | 0x3500 | 0x1700 | 0x800 |
| main | 28,672 | 229,376 | 0x3400 | 0x1600 | 0x700 |

The linear levels now use the same rounded-up extent as the tiled ones, for the pitch and for the level's rows. A test in `RunTextureTilingTests` pins addrlib's values for that volume.

How it was found: AnyPS5's `TextureTiling.cpp` was compared against Mesa's addrlib, compiled unmodified and called through `Addr2ComputeSurfaceInfo` / `Addr2ComputeSurfaceAddrFromCoord`. The config was gfx1013, revision 0x82, GB_ADDR_CONFIG 0x00100044 (16 pipes).

### Tested

Windows 11 (26200), WinLibs GCC 15.2.0 r7, CI configure flags, main at 63c57d22:

- `agc_driver_graphics` (includes the tiling tests) passes on an RTX 4070 Laptop GPU and an Intel Raptor Lake-S iGPU. With the old rounding put back, it fails with `linear 8 bpp 100x60x8, 4 levels: slice size differs from addrlib`.

body:
> Investigated and written by Claude Code (AI), and posted by me after review.

> **Work in progress.** The number of frames kept (5) comes from an experiment with one game, not from console documentation. The right lifetime rule for a handed-out video frame needs review; see "Open question" below.

### What

A title that asks AvPlayer for 2 output video framebuffers (`num_output_video_framebuffers = 2`) got no protection for the frame it was shown last. In `Source.cpp`, `present` keeps `videoBuffers - 3` earlier handed-out frames, which is 0 for 2 or 3 buffers, so the previous frame's buffer goes back to the free list as soon as the next frame is handed out. `acquireBuffer` then takes the newest free buffer first, so the decoder writes the next decoded picture into exactly that buffer right away. AnyPS5's GPU work runs behind the game thread, and can still be reading that buffer for the frame the game already submitted.

In Hollow Knight: Silksong (PPSA12544) this shows in the intro cinematic: whole frames briefly jump back about 0.3 s (sometimes forward), and one frame was torn. Discussion: https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5/discussions/1519

The change:
- After the 4 optional decode-ahead framebuffers, the player asks the memory replacement for 4 more optional framebuffers. When it gets them, it keeps at least the 5 newest handed-out frames intact (the current one and 4 earlier ones). When memory is short, the behaviour is the same as before.
- Free framebuffers are reused oldest first instead of newest first, so a buffer that was just released is the last one to be written again.

The unknown console rule is recorded in `docs/dev/TechnicalDebt.md`.

#### Open question

The fix keeps a fixed number of frames; it does not know when the GPU has actually read a frame. AvPlayer has no link to the AGC driver today. A rule tied to GPU completion (for example waiting until the GPU work submitted before the next `GetVideoData` has finished before reusing a buffer) would be exact, but it needs a hook between the two libraries, and how the console itself handles this (how long a frame from `sceAvPlayerGetVideoData` stays valid) is not documented. Reviewers who know the console behaviour, or prefer the GPU-completion approach, are welcome to say so.

### Tested

Arch Linux, GCC, Release, `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`; Intel i7-8750H, GTX 1050 Ti Max-Q with NVIDIA 580.178.04. Rebased onto `main` 406b5e1c; the results below are on 406b5e1c unless marked as from the earlier base cba8d86d.

- `guest_avplayer`: new cases check that with 2 output buffers the 5 newest handed-out frames are not overwritten (and with 6 buffers), and that the 4 extra framebuffers are requested only when the texture memory allows. Passes; with only the `Source.cpp` change reverted it fails (checked on cba8d86d).
- Full `ctest -j4`: 482/482 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed, the same set as `main` 406b5e1c.
- Full suite under `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation` (on cba8d86d): 452/452 passed, 0 skipped; the same `Validation Error` VUIDs and counts as `main`.
- `tools/check_conventions.py --base 406b5e1c` and `tools/check_test_registration.py build`: pass.
- Silksong intro cinematic (before the rebase), window recordings counted with the same frame-comparison script (a frame that differs from both neighbours while the neighbours match each other):
  - before (`main` behaviour): 63 such events in about 130 s of cinematic (50 plain jumps, the rest around the cinematic's own flashes);
  - with an experimental switch that kept 4 more frames and reused buffers oldest first: 3 events (2 small jumps and 1 of the cinematic's own white flashes);
  - with this PR (on a local branch with other open PRs merged, which Silksong needs to run): the cinematic played through and the game reached gameplay and saved. The window-only recordings came out incomplete (other windows covered the game area, and the recorder captured only part of the cinematic), so they give no reliable count: 1 event in 58 s and 0 in 24 s of usable footage.
- With the change, the version text on the title screen and the "skip" prompt during the cinematic appear again (they were missing before).

Not changed by this PR: in the same cinematic the sound plays well ahead of the picture (the user estimates up to about a minute by the end). It was already there before this change, and the picture does not look slowed down, more like a growing or fixed offset. It is being investigated separately.

body:
> Investigated and written by Claude Code (AI), and posted by me after review.

### What

#904 made `sceKernelGetModuleInfoForUnwind` report a guest image's unwind tables on Windows. On Linux the call still answers `eh_frame_hdr_addr`, `eh_frame_addr` and `eh_frame_size` = 0 for every address. A title that ships its own `libc.prx` unwinds C++ exceptions with that libc's libunwind, which asks this call where a frame's FDEs are; with the empty answer it falls back to its list of registered frames, which is empty, so no C++ exception thrown in guest code can be caught on Linux.

PPSA12544 (Hollow Knight: Silksong) on Linux ends after its intro cinematic with the same message #904 fixed on Windows:

```
Terminating due to uncaught exception of type Il2CppExceptionWrapper
```

(reported in https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5/discussions/1519).

body:
### What

Fixes the boxed glyphs in PPSA12544's menus (finding 2 of #865).

`StorageTexture::writeBackLayers` keeps the CPU's bytes for a block the write watch stamped after the layer's generation, and drops the GPU results there. The write watch reports page writes, not changes. In #865 the stamped pages of the font atlas still hold the allocator fill (`0xCD`) the image was uploaded from, so the CPU changed nothing there, yet the glyphs the GPU drew into those pages are lost.

The keep decision now also asks whether the CPU changed the bytes:

- When an image's layers get their generation (`upload`, including the clear and import paths), images up to 1 MiB keep a copy of their guest bytes (`generationBaseline`). An image uploaded through the CPU snapshot already has it in `original`.
- A range that is stamped, but whose guest bytes still equal that copy, stores the GPU results. A range whose bytes differ keeps the CPU's bytes, as before.

A stale baseline (generation moved on without a new copy) can only make the comparison fail, which keeps the previous behaviour. Real CPU stores change bytes and still win. The direct (import) write-back path is unchanged: the decision only removes ranges from the CPU-kept set.

This is the range-level variant of the baseline comparison suggested in #865. @merwie's experiment there merges per byte and forces the CPU write-back path; this one keeps the existing paths and decides per stored range.

### Tested

- Windows 11, NVIDIA RTX 5090, MinGW GCC 15.2.0, Release.
- New `unchangedCpuStampTests` in `agc_driver_recorder_tests`: a 256x256 RGBA8 linear image at +0x2000 in watched memory (so its first unit is an edge block), cleared on the GPU and marked dirty, then the CPU rewrites the first page.
  - CPU rewrote the same bytes: every texel is stored. Without the fix: `dropped 14336 of 65536 texels the GPU wrote` (the 0xe000-byte head edge).
  - CPU changed one byte: that byte keeps the CPU's value, the GPU results past the head block are stored.
- `ctest`: 456 of 456 passed. `agc_driver_recorder_tests` (run directly, as it needs the GPU): passed.
- PPSA12544 (Hollow Knight: Silksong) on Windows, with #846, #1482, #1495 and #788 applied for bring-up: the title menu, Options and Game Options render without boxed letters or digits, and `APS5_TRACE_FLUSH=1` reports no CPU-kept blocks. No eager write-back.

### What

Adds `--macos` to the relinker: the executable and the bundled modules are written as x86-64 Mach-O files (modules as dylibs in `app0/sce_module`) that run under Rosetta on Apple silicon. This is the second piece of the macOS port after #927, as announced on #1 (https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5/issues/1#issuecomment-6060813714).

- `MacOsMachOPatcher` writes the executable and `GuestModuleWriter::WriteMacOs` the modules, both through `MacOsImage`. The ELF segments keep their layout (`__ELF0`, `__ELF1`, ...). Imports bind by NID to the prx libraries through `@rpath`, exports and TLS imports use the dynamic symbol names, and the original program headers and the image metadata go to `__APS5DATA,__meta`, the section the unwinder from #927 reads.
- FreeBSD code reaches its thread pointer through `%fs`, which macOS cannot set. Each `%fs` access becomes a stub that reads the thread pointer from a pthread key and allocates the TLS block on a thread's first access; dynamic TLS goes through the image's descriptor instead of `__tls_get_addr`.
- Relocations and imports are collected with the existing `Windows::WindowsLoadImage` and `WindowsRelocationBuilder`. Moving them to `general/` is a refactor for a follow-up.
- `--macos` conflicts with `--windows`. `--to-intel` with `--macos` still uses the Intel target here; the Rosetta target comes in its own PR.

The Linux and Windows output is unchanged. The Mach-O output needs the macOS runtime (TLS allocation in libkernel, libraries built for macOS), which comes in separate PRs.

body:
### What

`DecodeRdnaMubuf` reads `OFFEN`, `IDXEN`, `GLC`, `DLC` and `SLC`, but not bit 16 of word 0, `LDS`. AMD's RDNA2 machine-readable ISA lays out MUBUF word 0 as `OFFSET[11:0] OFFEN[12] IDXEN[13] GLC[14] DLC[15] LDS[16] OP[24:18]` and describes the bit as "If set, data is read from/written to LDS memory".

So a `buffer_load_dword ... lds` decodes exactly like a VGPR load: the recompiled program writes VDATA and never fills LDS.

FLAT already refuses its own `lds` bit (`unsupported FLAT modifiers or segment`). MUBUF now throws `unsupported MUBUF lds modifier`.

`agc_mubuf_lds_decode` decodes `buffer_load_dword v1, off, s[4:7], 0`, expecting `BufferLoadDword`, and the same encoding with `lds` set, expecting the error.

How it was found: every RDNA2 instruction in the XML (1465) was decoded with `RdnaInstructionDecoder`. Opcode mappings and lengths all match, and the encoding fields were flipped one at a time to find bits the decoder ignores. Two turned up:

- `LDS`, fixed here.
- MUBUF/MTBUF `TFE` (word 1 bit 23), left as it is. With always-resident memory there is no residency status to return, as for MIMG in #616.

### Tested

Windows 11 (26200), WinLibs GCC 15.2.0 r7, CI configure flags, main at b3fcd6d6 (rebased on 1e660dd9):

- `agc_mubuf_lds_decode` passes. With the new check replaced by a no-op, it fails: `buffer_load_dword off, s[4:7], 0 lds decodes as a VGPR load`.
- Full suite on NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop (driver 32.0.15.9597): 454/454 passed.

### What

Related to #1471 (the empty-registration `sceNetEpollWait` path only).

With the supported WinLibs toolchain, `std::condition_variable::wait_until` uses winpthreads' coarse `GetTickCount64` deadline. A 1,000 us empty epoll wait can therefore take approximately one 15.6 ms tick despite the process requesting a 0.5 ms timer resolution.

Use a translation-unit-local Windows SRW lock and native condition variable for the network registry. Preserve the existing steady-clock deadline, 100 ms polling slices, wake-all notifications, socket lifetimes and guest error behavior. Linux retains `std::mutex` and `std::condition_variable`. Unexpected native wait failures throw, matching the project's exact-or-throw policy.

Extend `GuestSceNet.cpp` with empty finite and zero waits, abort consumption, abort/destroy of indefinite waits, and adding a readable socket to a waiting epoll instance. The timing regression checks the median of nine 1 ms waits rather than imposing a bound on every sample.

### Tested

Windows 11 Home 10.0.26300, supported WinLibs GCC 15.2.0 UCRT POSIX SEH r7; WSL Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, GCC 15.2.0. Release builds, `BUILD_TESTING=ON`, at most two compiler jobs, based on upstream `fd5342b6`.

- Original Windows implementation: 40 requests for 1,000 us had a 15.494 ms median; the new regression failed. Original Linux functional regression passed.
- Final Windows patched PRX: 40 requests had a 1.492 ms median; final Linux patched PRX: 1.099 ms. Every probe request waited at least 1 ms and returned zero events.
- Nine relevant CTest cases, three consecutive passes each on both platforms: 54 passes, zero failures/skips. Cases: `guest_sce_net`, `guest_tcp`, `guest_udp`, `guest_poll`, `guest_addresses`, `guest_cond_timedwait`, `guest_nanosleep`, `guest_pthread_sem`, `guest_sync_on_address`.
- Windows `guest_sce_net` also passed with `APS5_COARSE_TIMED_WAITS=1` and `APS5_NO_TIMER_RESOLUTION=1`: two additional passes. The latter intentionally omits the latency ceiling while retaining the timeout lower bound and all functional checks. Its 15.558 ms median reproduced an independent review finding, which the corrected test guard resolves.
- Repository convention checker, PR template check, test-registration checker on both platforms, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Built and NID-patched `libc`, `libkernel`, `libSceNet` and `libSceNetCtl`, then loaded the patched network library and invoked its epoll exports by NID on both platforms. Used the repository's patcher and the same `--preserve-exports` input as CMake; the generated packaging target's unrelated dependency fan-out was cancelled.


body:
### What

`Driver::preparePacketMemory` reads `packet[2]`, the `RELEASE_MEM` interrupt select, for every packet. The read used to sit behind `opcode == 0x49 &&`, and #1362 moved it ahead of that check. `packet` is the packet's own span, and `Pm4::Validate` accepts 2-dword packets, for example `PFP_SYNC_ME` (`case 0x42: size(2)`). So for those, index 2 is one past the end:

- In a normal build it reads the next packet's header. If the 2-dword packet is the last one in the submission, it reads 4 bytes past the end of the command buffer.
- The value is only used when the opcode is `0x49`, so the result is unaffected, but the read is out of bounds.
- With `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS`, the `std::span` bounds check aborts on the first such packet.

The interrupt select is now read only for `RELEASE_MEM`, whose packet `Validate` requires to be 8 dwords.

### Tested

Windows 11 (26200), WinLibs GCC 15.2.0 r7.

- Build with `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS -fsanitize=undefined -fsanitize-trap=undefined` (main at 0596a7a2), NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop:

  - With it, both pass.

body:
### What

`agc_driver_many_buffers` fails on Apple GPUs with "shader descriptors exceed per-stage limits". MoltenVK reports `maxPerStageDescriptorStorageBuffers` 31 and `maxDescriptorSetStorageBuffers` 155 on every Apple GPU, while the test binds 124 buffers in one stage. its update-after-bind limits are 1000000, and the guest buffers are one constant-indexed array binding, so the shaders don't need to change

when a stage's storage buffers or resources go above the regular per-stage limit, or the set's storage buffers above the per-set limit, and the device has `descriptorBindingStorageBufferUpdateAfterBind`, the set now uses the update-after-bind limits instead of throwing

- `VulkanDevice` enables `descriptorBindingStorageBufferUpdateAfterBind` when available and passes `VkPhysicalDeviceDescriptorIndexingProperties` through the context. without the feature those limits stay 0 and the old error is thrown
- such a set's layout gets `UPDATE_AFTER_BIND_POOL` with `UPDATE_AFTER_BIND` on its storage-buffer bindings, and is allocated from a separate chain of pools created with `UPDATE_AFTER_BIND`. the layout key carries the flag. the two places that created layouts share `CreateSetLayout` now, and the two that created single-set pools share `CreateSetPool`
- a set within the regular limits takes the same path as before, so devices with large limits, like the AMD, NVIDIA and lavapipe ones, are unchanged
- image bindings after an update-after-bind buffer binding are checked against the update-after-bind resource limit
- `ValidateDescriptorLayout`, added on main since this PR was opened, takes the same flag and checks such a set against `maxPerStageUpdateAfterBindResources` instead of `maxPerStageResources`

### Tested

- macOS 15.6.1 on an M1 Pro, MoltenVK from Vulkan SDK 1.4.363.0, on top of mugurc's `macos-port` branch, before the rebase. `agc_driver_many_buffers` fails before and passes after. the rest of the suite ran with `-j1 --timeout 30` without the flip and display tests and `agc_driver_lds_atomics64`. 427 tests, and the 2 that fail, `agc_driver_pixel_interlock` and `agc_driver_sdwa_float_selectors`, fail the same way without this change

body:
### What
Addresses the sub-millisecond sleep busy-spin issue documented in #1471:
On Windows, `std::this_thread::sleep_for` goes through winpthreads' `nanosleep`, which truncates sub-millisecond durations (`tv_nsec / 1'000'000`) to 0 ms and returns immediately without sleeping or yielding. As a result, polling loops requesting sub-millisecond pauses spin at 100% CPU.

This PR switches the sub-millisecond host waits in four areas to use `PreciseSleepUs()` (which uses a Windows high-resolution waitable timer `CREATE_WAITABLE_TIMER_HIGH_RESOLUTION` on Windows and standard microsecond sleep on POSIX):
- `core/libs/prx/libSceAgcDriver/Execution/src/Pm4.cpp`: `WAIT_REG_MEM` polling loop (50 µs)
- `core/libs/prx/libkernel/Apr/src/Apr.cpp`: `_execute` counter and address wait loop (50 µs)
- `core/libs/prx/libkernel/Aio/src/Aio.cpp`: `sceKernelAioWaitRequests` and `sceKernelAioWaitRequest` polling loops (10 µs)
- `core/libs/prx/libSceFont/src/State.cpp`: `Font::Backoff` spinlock backoff (30 µs)

### What

`agc_driver_vop1_float_unary` fails on an Apple M1 with `exp_f32` of -126 giving 0 where the test expects `0x00800000`. the M1 GPU's `exp2` comes out about 2 ULP low even for whole numbers (2^-120 gives `0x037ffffe`), checked in plain Metal with fast math on and off. at -126 that lands just under the normal range, and Metal flushes it to 0

body:
### What

Unity's stop-the-world collector can raise `SIGUSR1` while a worker is inside a host mutex wait. The previous Windows path could remain blocked in MinGW's TLS implementation: the signal handler re-entered guest thread state, pthread TSD or `TimedWait` state while the interrupted code still held an internal MinGW TLS lock. That left the collector waiting for a thread that could not run its handler and produced repeated `sce::Agc::suspendPoint` messages associated with the TRC R5089 watchdog.

This change keeps the signal-visible state out of MinGW TLS on Windows:

- guest current-thread state and pthread TSD use native Windows FLS;
- `TimedWait` state and per-thread timers use the same FLS-backed storage;
- a contended `scePthreadMutexLock` uses short alertable waits through `try_lock`, allowing the GC delivery path to run while the mutex owner is still held;
- blocking read/write rwlock waits use the same interruptible polling path;
- the existing Linux paths retain `thread_local` storage and the existing condition-variable implementation.

The default mutex type change (`ErrorCheck` to `Normal`) was removed after it caused a `guest_kernel_errors` regression. It belongs in a separate change.

A permanent Vulkan `WaitIdle` was intentionally not added. Forcing Vulkan idle did not remove the loading stall, so `suspendPoint` is fixed at the thread-synchronization layer.

This PR complements [#1476](https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5/pull/1476), which fixes nested `TimedWait` waiter ownership. The measured PPSA28997 freeze requires both parts.

### Tests

Added `guest_mutex_raise_exception`, a Windows regression test that:

- holds a mutex from the main thread;
- blocks a worker in `scePthreadMutexLock`;
- raises `SIGUSR1` on the blocked worker;
- verifies handler delivery;
- releases the mutex and verifies that the worker acquires, releases and joins successfully.

### Tested

God of War: Sons of Sparta (PPSA28997), Windows 10, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080.

The game reached the normal menu with the shader cache populated. The repeated `Forcing call to sce::Agc::suspendPoint to avoid TRC R5089 breach` loop did not recur during the verified run.

Targeted Windows tests: `guest_raise_exception`, `guest_mutex_raise_exception` and `guest_pthread_key`. CI runs the complete platform test suites.

body:
### What

`LinuxElfPatcher` wrote the program header table as PT_PHDR, the header-block PT_LOAD, the kept original headers, the extra-block PT_LOAD, PT_DYNAMIC and PT_INTERP. The header block is placed after the extra block, so it has the highest address of all loadable segments while being the first PT_LOAD entry in the table. The ELF gABI requires loadable segment entries to appear in ascending `p_vaddr` order, and PT_PHDR and PT_INTERP to precede every loadable entry.

Linux before 5.18 sizes the ET_DYN mapping as `last PT_LOAD p_vaddr + p_memsz - page_start(first PT_LOAD p_vaddr)` in table order (`total_mapping_size`, `fs/binfmt_elf.c` v5.15). For a relinked executable that difference underflows, `elf_map` fails after the point of no return, and the process dies with SIGSEGV before the dynamic linker runs. On 5.18 and later the kernel takes the minimum and maximum over all PT_LOAD entries, so the file loads, but the first mapping still reserves the range starting at the header block instead of the lowest segment.

Kernel coverage, from `fs/binfmt_elf.c` of each release:

| Kernel | `main` | This pull request |
|---|---|---|
| 5.18 and later | runs | runs |
| 5.15.33 to 5.17, 5.10.110 and later stable (WSL2 5.15.167 included) | SIGSEGV at exec | runs |
| 5.15.0 to 5.15.32, 5.10.109 and earlier | SIGSEGV at exec | still fails |

The last row lacks the backport of the 5.18 AT_PHDR fix, so `AT_PHDR` is computed as the first PT_LOAD's `p_vaddr - p_offset` plus `e_phoff`. That points into the header block only while the header block is the first PT_LOAD, which is exactly the order the table-order `total_mapping_size` rejects. Supporting those kernels would need the program header table moved to a segment whose file-to-address delta matches the lowest PT_LOAD; that is a separate change. No kernel runs `main` and fails with this pull request.

`ProgramHeaderLayoutBuilder::WriteLayout` now writes PT_PHDR, PT_INTERP, the kept original headers with their PT_LOAD entries sorted by `p_vaddr` (the Windows image builder already sorts them in `WindowsLoadImage`), the extra-block PT_LOAD, the header-block PT_LOAD and PT_DYNAMIC. The guest module writer already orders its segments this way.

Rebased on `main` after #1586 merged: its `PT_GNU_EH_FRAME` slot check and warning are kept, and a dropped `PT_GNU_EH_FRAME` is removed from the kept headers before they are laid out.

### Tested

WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 5.15.167.4-microsoft-standard-WSL2, glibc 2.39, GCC 13.3), Linux build with `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`.

- Before the change `linux_entry_argv` fails there: the output exits with SIGSEGV (-11) instead of SIGTRAP. Reordering the PT_LOAD entries of that output by hand makes it run, which isolated the cause.
- After the change the full suite passes on current `main`: 514/514 with `ctest --test-dir build -j8` (23 GPU tests skipped by the WSL Vulkan device), including `linux_entry_argv`, `linux_eh_frame_header` and the new test.
- The same Build workflow on the fork for the previous head (stacked on #1586): Linux 457/457, Windows 449/449 (https://github.com/ctj01/AnyPS5/actions/runs/37812797526).
- New `linux_program_header_order` test: a single-segment image, a three-segment image (text, rodata, data with bss) with a kept PT_OS_PROCPARAM entry, and the same image with its PT_LOAD entries out of order in the input. It checks PT_PHDR first, PT_INTERP before the first PT_LOAD, strictly ascending PT_LOAD addresses, the preserved non-load entry, that the 5.15 table-order span equals the address span, that PT_PHDR is covered by a PT_LOAD, and on Linux x86-64 it executes the outputs and expects SIGTRAP from the entry.

body:
### What

`InstructionScanner` sweeps code linearly with `X64InstructionDecoder::Decode`, so one wrong length puts the rest of the sweep out of step (#1162, #1167). `decoderLengths` checks about 40 hand-picked encodings. This adds `decoder_length`: 946 encodings whose lengths come from LLVM's x86 disassembler, each checked three ways:

- `Decode` on a buffer of exactly the instruction returns its length;
- the same with 15 NOPs after it;
- one byte short throws `CodegenException` (no read past the end).

`tools/x86_decoder_cases.py` regenerates `DecoderLengthCases.hpp`: it builds every one-byte, `0F`, `0F 38` and `0F 3A` opcode with no prefix, `66`, `F2`, `F3`, `REX.W`, `66 REX.W` and `67`, and every VEX map 1-3 opcode for each `pp`, `L` and `W`, each with a register ModRM and a SIB + disp32 memory ModRM. It has `llvm-objdump` decode them and keeps one case per opcode for each distinct length, plus all four operand-size prefix combinations where they change the length. It skips encodings LLVM rejects, VMREAD/VMWRITE (`0F 78`/`0F 79` without an SSE4a prefix, which the decoder rejects on purpose) and `66`-prefixed near branches, whose length differs between Intel (ignored) and AMD (rel16). Its output is deterministic.

The table catches the three length bugs fixed today: run against the decoder of each earlier revision, it fails with `Wrong length for 66480584651122` before #1163, and `Cannot decode 0fa8: Instruction truncated before ModRM byte` before #1381; MOV moffs (`a1…`, `67 a1…`) fails before #1168. On current `main` all 946 pass.

### Tested
On macOS (Apple clang, arm64): `decoder_length_tests` built from `DecoderLengthTests.cpp` and `X64InstructionDecoder.cpp` with only the two include directories the CMake target lists, `-Wall -Wextra` clean, passes on `main`; built against the decoder at `2959dc53` and `e66d78c6` it fails as described. A second LLVM pass over the table, with `int3` padding, agrees with every length. `tools/check_conventions.py --base origin/main` passes. Running the generator again reproduces the header byte for byte (`--objdump objdump --clang clang` with Xcode's LLVM 21). No x86-64 toolchain on this machine, so the Linux and Windows builds are left to CI.

body:
### What

Replace sub-millisecond `std::this_thread::sleep_for` polling with `PreciseSleepUs()` in four host-side loops. On Windows, winpthreads truncates these `nanosleep` requests to whole milliseconds, so requests below 1 ms return immediately and spin. This addresses the Windows busy-spin behavior documented in #1471.

- AGC `WAIT_REG_MEM`: 50 µs
- APR counter/address wait: 50 µs
- AIO wait requests: 10 µs
- Font lock backoff: 30 µs

Keep the focused `precise_wait` CTest for the helper. The four production changes from #1576 are included here, with Shaan credited as co-author.

### Tested

- Linux x86_64, GCC 12.2, Release: configured with `BUILD_TESTING=ON`; built `precise_wait_tests`, `guest_ampr_tests`, `guest_aio_tests`, `guest_font_tests`, `guest_font_writing_line_tests`, `agc_driver_graphics_tests`, and `agc_driver_pm4_tests`.
- Focused CTest: 7/7 passed (`precise_wait`, `agc_driver_graphics`, `agc_driver_pm4_failure`, `guest_ampr_markers`, `guest_aio`, `guest_font`, `guest_font_writing_line`).
- `tools/check_conventions.py --base upstream/main` and `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` pass.
- A contributor's Windows 10 / MinGW GCC 15.2 report on the same four call sites measured `sleep_for(10/50/200 µs)` returning immediately and `PreciseSleepUs` taking about 0.5 ms; see [the report](https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5/pull/1576#issuecomment-6077516702). An independent Windows 11 Pro 25H2 report on the exact source diff (PR commit `d6c7e2f6` cherry-picked onto current `main` `d70b8998`) used RTX 5060 Ti / NVIDIA 617.42, MinGW-w64 GCC 15.2.0, Release and a full build plus `libs`: `precise_wait` passed and full CTest passed (511/511), including `guest_aio`, `guest_ampr_markers`, `guest_font`, `guest_font_writing_line` and `agc_driver_pm4_failure` ([report](https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5/pull/1551#issuecomment-6081053209)).
- In that contributor's AIO workload, both waits returned on their first check, so no AIO performance improvement is claimed; the change prevents a zero-duration spin if those polling paths do wait.

- `FileAndHeap.cpp` (`-Wignored-attributes`, 1 on Linux): `decltype(&std::fclose)` carries glibc's attributes into the `unique_ptr` deleter type; the deleter is now `int (*)(std::FILE*)`.
- `Ajm.cpp` (`-Wnonnull`, 13 on Linux): `Append` is inlined into the batch-job functions that pass `nullptr` buffers, and the fortified `memcpy` warned about them. `Append` now throws (`NotImplemented_nid_no_patch`) when a buffer list is null and its count is not zero, since the console's result there is unknown, and copies only when the pointer is set. `sceAjmBatchJobRunSplit` with `nullptr` inputs and a count of 1 used to crash in `memcpy`; `GuestAjm.cpp` checks that it now throws and leaves the batch untouched.

- `LookBackScan.cpp` (`-Wstringop-overflow` / `-Warray-bounds` from `std::vector::insert`, Linux only), a GCC false positive in a test.

body:
### What

Without `VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric` (lavapipe in CI, NVIDIA before Turing, older Intel), the recompiler dropped `v_interp_p1_f32` and had `v_interp_p2_f32` read the attribute Vulkan interpolated, but it never wrote the I/J VGPRs. So on `main`:

- a pixel shader that reads I/J for anything other than `v_interp_p1/p2` of the same pair (EvaluateAttributeAt*-style offsets, custom weights, exporting them) silently gets 0;
- `v_interp_mov_f32` of P10/P20, or of P0 of an interpolated input, needs `PerVertexKHR` and fails pipeline validation ("device does not support enabled VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric");
- inputs that share a slot with different interpolation fail the same way.

This removes the silent stub listed in TechnicalDebt and replaces it with exact emulation:

1. **Translation.** The fallback now loads I/J like the barycentric path. `v_interp_p1_f32` writes an `InterpolateHostP1` witness, and `v_interp_p2_f32` adds a side-effecting `InterpolateHostP2(attr, chan, J, partial)` witness before its usual host-interpolated write.
2. **`HostInterpolationChecker`**, which runs after the SSA/fold/DCE/read-lane/masked-select passes:
   - It checks that every P2 reads its J, and that its p1's I comes from a barycentric of the parameter's kind.
   - It checks that every p1 result only reaches the matching p2, either directly or through a write masked by the p2's EXEC.
   - It checks that no parameter is read as raw vertices and no slot mixes interpolations.
   - It then lowers the witnesses: the masked p1 write keeps the old register value in inactive lanes, as on the barycentric path.
   - It reruns DCE and masked-select elimination, and accepts the program only if no barycentric read remains.
   - Accepted programs give the same SPIR-V as before. Overwriting or accumulating into the I/J VGPRs after the interpolation stays on this path.
3. **Emulated programs.** Anything else is translated with the barycentric semantics and marked as emulated:
   - `BaryCoordKHR`/`BaryCoordNoPerspKHR` become `vec3` inputs; the linear one is `NoPerspective`.
   - `PerVertexKHR` parameters become `Flat vec4[3]` inputs.
   - These inputs take the free locations chosen by `LayoutBarycentricEmulation`.
   - `RecompileResult::barycentricEmulation` records this; the shader disk cache format goes to 8.
4. **`BuildBarycentricGeometryShader`** generates a pass-through geometry stage: triangles in, a three-vertex strip out. It copies the position and the plain parameters, writes the one-hot weights (1,0,0)/(0,1,0)/(0,0,1), and copies the three vertices' values into each per-vertex array. The rasterizer then interpolates exactly the weights `BaryCoordKHR` gives, with the same vertex order (`gl_in[0]` stays the provoking vertex). The driver inserts the stage between the vertex and fragment shaders, like the rect-list stages. `ValidateShaders` accepts `[Vertex, Geometry, Fragment]` only for an emulated fragment shader and triangle topologies. The pipeline and validation keys treat the stage as generated, and `Pipeline` requires `geometryShader`.

**Limits.** Tessellation, mesh and rect-list pipelines with such a shader throw, as do other primitive types, more than 32 fragment input locations, and interfaces past the device's geometry limits. These limits are recorded in TechnicalDebt.

**Behaviour that does not change:**
- Devices with the extension are unaffected: the checker and the SPIR-V changes run only without it.
- Shaders that only use `v_interp_p1/p2` keep host interpolation and their previous SPIR-V.

Sources:
- `v_interp_p1_f32`/`v_interp_p2_f32`/`v_interp_mov_f32` (P0, P10, P20, I/J): AMD "RDNA 2" Instruction Set Architecture, section "Parameter Interpolation".
- Barycentric weights and per-vertex order: [SPV_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric](https://github.khronos.org/SPIRV-Registry/extensions/KHR/SPV_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric.html), `VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric`.
- Triangle vertex order into a geometry shader and the provoking vertex: Vulkan specification, "Primitive Topologies" and "Geometry Shading".
- Interpolation decided by the fragment input decoration: Vulkan specification, "Interpolation Decorations".

### Tested
Ubuntu (Linux 7.0, GCC 15.2.0), Release, `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`, lavapipe (Mesa, LLVM 21), which has no `VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric` but has `geometryShader`. No title or hardware GPU.

- **New `agc_driver_pixel_barycentric_emulation`** (GPU, lavapipe). It draws a triangle whose vertices have w = 1, 2.5 and 0.5 into a 64x48 R32G32B32A32 float target:
  - A pixel shader that exports `v0, v1` with PERSP_CENTER, then with LINEAR_CENTER, matches the perspective-correct and the screen-space barycentrics computed on the CPU within 2.5e-4 at all 932 interior pixels (hardware snaps window vertices to 1/256 pixel before computing the weights, lavapipe does not).
  - `v_interp_mov_f32` P10, P20 and P0 of an interpolated input give exactly `x1-x0`, `x2-x0` and `x0`.
  - Plain `v_interp_p1/p2` keeps host interpolation and matches the perspective-correct value.
  - On `main` the same exports read 0 at every pixel (e.g. pixel (32,24): 0 0 0 0, expected I=0.137, J=0.717), and the `v_interp_mov` draw throws.

body:
### What

Proposed replacement for #1479: retain the ClearMRT color outputs while clearing stencil, with writable-plane validation and regression coverage. The original implementation is included as a separate commit with Aryan Sharma's authorship preserved. This PR is standalone and does not require #1479 to merge first.

`DB_RENDER_CONTROL = 0x22` sets `STENCIL_CLEAR_ENABLE`, not depth clear. Rejecting the whole draw drops its color writes as well. In God of War Sons of Sparta (PPSA28997), the uncleared scene target accumulates the previous frames' lighting and develops growing white highlights.

Rasterize the existing draw with `ALWAYS` comparison and stencil `REPLACE` on both faces, using `DB_STENCIL_CLEAR`. This retains color exports, write masks and scissor coverage. No extra GPU pass, allocation or synchronization is introduced.

Compared with #1479:

- Require a present, writable stencil plane; read-only stencil and absent planes throw, including when both depth/stencil formats are disabled. The draw precheck also rejects invalid clear targets.
- Select stencil-clear state before decoding ordinary stencil operations. Operations overridden by the clear can otherwise reject a valid draw before the replacement is applied.
- Cover two color attachments with different write masks, scissor coverage, both stencil faces, disabled/enabled stencil tests, read-only depth, and continued rejection of depth clear/copy operations.

Register definitions: [AMD PAL DB_RENDER_CONTROL](https://github.com/GPUOpen-Drivers/pal/blob/dev/src/core/hw/gfxip/gfx9/chip/gfx9_plus_merged_registers.h); clear/read-only view setup: [AMD PAL DepthStencilView::InitRegistersCommon](https://github.com/GPUOpen-Drivers/pal/blob/dev/src/core/hw/gfxip/gfx9/gfx9DepthStencilView.cpp). Vulkan replacement uses the reference value as specified by [VkStencilOp](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/VkStencilOp.html). No shader instruction semantics are changed.

### Tested

- Windows 10, NVIDIA RTX 3080, God of War Sons of Sparta (PPSA28997): the local ClearMRT fix removes the accumulating white highlights in the title/menu screen and retains normal brightness on subsequent frames. Before/after captures from that game check are below.
- MinGW-w64 GCC, Release: `agc_driver_graphics` passes after rebasing both commits onto `main` at `b1c5f10d`.
- The new read-only stencil regression fails on #1479's original implementation. Adding only the read-only guard exposes a second failure: an overridden stencil add operation rejects the clear. Both pass with this change.
- `tools/check_conventions.py --base origin/main` and `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` pass.

The automated tests validate decoded graphics state; they do not read back rendered GPU pixels. The game captures demonstrate the underlying ClearMRT fix, rather than an A/B comparison of the additional validation changes. Their resolutions differ, and they are not an FPS benchmark.

Before:

![Before: accumulating white highlights in God of War Sons of Sparta](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cdfffdbb-059e-4d5f-b4d6-12c153356b43)

After:

![After: title screen with normal lighting after the ClearMRT fix](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a8078554-f178-4f4b-a8c3-0e789376b28e)

### What

Additional content was never available: `sceAppContentAddcontMount` returned `NOT_FOUND` for every label, `sceAppContentGetAddcontInfo` `DRM_NO_ENTITLEMENT`, and the list was empty (TechnicalDebt, Functional).

- A catalog in libkernel (`AppMetadata/src/Addcont.cpp`, `AddcontEntries_nid_no_patch`) lists the title's add-ons once:
  - add-ons without data: labels from `anyps5-entitlements.ini` (`ANYPS5_ENTITLEMENTS`), read as `libSceNpEntitlementAccess` read them before;
  - add-ons with data: the subdirectories of `anyps5-addcont/` beside the executable (`ANYPS5_ADDCONT`), each named by its entitlement label or its content ID (`UP0000-PPSA00000_00-LABEL`). A label in both is one add-on with data.
  - Order: ini order, then directories sorted by label. An invalid directory name, two directories with one label, or a missing path named by an environment variable throws. Files in `anyps5-addcont/` are ignored.
- `libSceAppContent`:
  - `GetAddcontInfo` / `GetAddcontInfoList` report the catalog: status 4 (installed) for add-ons with data, 0 (no extra data) without. The list reports the count when called without a buffer, otherwise the entries written.
  - `AddcontMount` maps an add-on with data to `/addcont0` … `/addcont63` (lowest free slot) through `AddPathAlias_nid_no_patch`, as save data does for `/savedata0`. A second mount of the same add-on returns `BUSY`, a 65th mount `MOUNT_FULL`; an add-on without data or an unknown label `NOT_FOUND`.
  - `AddcontUnmount` blocks the point again with `BlockPathAlias_nid_no_patch` (as #1320 does for `/temp0`); a point that is not mounted returns `NOT_MOUNTED` (was `NOT_FOUND`). `/addcont0` … `/addcont63` are blocked from `sceAppContentInitialize` (or the first mount call) until mounted, so a path under an unmounted point fails instead of reaching the run directory.
- `libSceNpEntitlementAccess` reports the same catalog: ini entries as before (package type 3, download status 4), directories as package type 2 (PSAC). A label listed twice in the ini is now listed once.

Sources: error codes and limits from the PS4 SDK values in [ps4-eboot-dlc-patcher](https://github.com/idlesauce/ps4-eboot-dlc-patcher/blob/main/prx_src/libSceAppContent.h); the BUSY / MOUNT_FULL / NOT_MOUNTED cases and package types from the PS5 replacement modules in [dlc_emu](https://github.com/drakmor/dlc_emu); `/addcontN` names, status 0 for license-only add-ons and the list count from [shadPS4](https://github.com/shadps4-emu/shadPS4/blob/main/src/core/libraries/app_content/app_content.cpp) (PS4). body:
### What
Fixes #1497.

On Linux, `GuestModuleBuilder` renamed every import whose NID a guest module exports to its guest-suffixed name, whatever module the import declares: the executable's imports (`GuestModuleBuilder.cpp:180` on `main`) and the guest modules' own (`:218`). A title that bundles a module exporting system NIDs then had those imports bound to it.

DOOM PPSA99666 declares `snprintf`, `vsnprintf`, `strlen`, `memcpy`, `malloc` and `fopen` from `libSceLibcInternal` (`#G#H`, module 7) and nothing from `libc`. The `libc.prx` loader shim it bundles (ps5-native-app-boilerplate) exports placeholder functions under the same NIDs, so 71 imports became `<nid>#guest` and returned 0: no notification text, 27 opens of uninitialized paths, no WAD. Windows already binds by the declared module (`WindowsEntryStubBuilder`) and was not affected.

An import now binds to a guest export only when the module it declares is a guest module:

- Executable imports: the declared module of each symbol comes from `ImportModules` through its relocation. A symbol declared from a module that is not a guest keeps its plain name and binds to the host library.
- Guest-module imports: the same rule with `GuestSymbol::Library`; such an import is not searched among guest exports, renamed, or counted as a guest dependency.
- Unchanged: imports without import-module metadata, imports declared from a guest module (a title's own `libc.prx` imported from `libc` still binds to it, as in 7103f390 and `test_guest_host_libc.py`), and Windows (`declaresHost` is false there).

`test_guest_symbol_names` gets two cases, using the qualified-import fixtures from `test_windows_import_modules`: an executable that declares one NID from `libc` (a guest) and one from `libSceLibcInternal` (a host), both exported by the guest `libc.prx`; and a guest module importing `shared` from `libSceLibcInternal` while another guest exports it. On `main` the first fails with `{'EEEEEEEEEEE#guest', 'AAAAAAAAAAA#guest'}`.

Overlap: #1462 edits the lines next to the executable import loop, so whichever merges second needs a small rebase. #1403 and #1249 merge cleanly.

### Tested
- Linux (Ubuntu 24.04.5, GCC 13.3, RX 7600): full `ctest` 433/433, and the 152 guest/relinker tests again on the final revision; `guest_symbol_names` fails on `main` with the new cases and passes with this change.

body:
### What

`sceSystemServiceLoadExec("/app0/eboot.bin", argv)` restarts the running title with the given arguments instead of throwing. Only `"exit"` was handled before.

- The argument array is null-terminated and does not include the program name, as [shadPS4](https://github.com/shadps4-emu/shadPS4) reads it (`src/core/libraries/system/systemservice.cpp`). The restarted title keeps the host `argv[0]`. Neither point is confirmed on a PS5 title; both are recorded in TechnicalDebt.
- Any other executable still throws, because the relinker converts only the title's executable.
- **Linux**: after the runtime shutdown (`LibcRunShutdown`), descriptors above 2 are marked close-on-exec, the signal mask and ignored signals are reset, and `execv("/proc/self/exe", ...)` replaces the process. The PID stays the same.
- **Windows**: there is no process replacement. The new process gets an inherited `SYNCHRONIZE` handle to the old one, named by `ANYPS5_LOAD_EXEC_PREVIOUS_PROCESS`. libSceSystemService waits on it while loading, before the title runs. The old process runs the shutdown and then terminates. The two processes therefore never hold direct memory at the same time, which matters because it is committed in full (USAGE.md). Arguments are passed as UTF-8, the same encoding the entry stub uses, and are quoted by the `CommandLineToArgvW` rules. Arguments that are not UTF-8 throw before anything is started.

### Tested

- **Windows 10 22H2 (19045)**, RTX 4060, WinLibs GCC 15.2.0 UCRT r7, Release, `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`
  - The new `guest_load_exec_restart` restarts `guest_system_exit_tests` with `two words`, `quote"d`, `trailing\`, `back\\"slash`, `ü` and an empty argument. The restarted process checks that each argument arrives byte for byte, and that the old process had ended before it ran. The test's shutdown callback sleeps 500 ms, so a missing wait would be caught.
  - The 6 exit tests passed 10 times out of 10.
  - Deleting the wait makes the test fail.
  - The full suite passes 429 of 430. The one failure is `agc_driver_srgb8_color_target`, which is #1434 (addressed by the open #1441): it fails in 20 of 30 runs on `main` on this machine, and in 0 of 30 with that issue's `Sleep(50)` experiment. Its binary loads only libc, libkernel and libSceAgcDriver, none of which this PR changes.
- **Linux, Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2)**, GCC 13.3, Release
  - The same test passed 10 times out of 10. The restarted process has the same PID. Before the restart, the old process ignores `SIGPIPE` and blocks `SIGUSR1`; the restarted process checks that both are back to their defaults.
  - Dropping an argument, skipping the shutdown, skipping the signal reset, or resetting only the mask each make it fail.
  - With `--coverage`, the test runs 32 of the 34 lines of the Linux half of `LoadExec.cpp`. The two lines not run are a `pthread_sigmask` failure path and the unreachable closing brace.
  - The full suite on lavapipe (Mesa 25.2.8, `VK_DRIVER_FILES`, `GALLIUM_OVERRIDE_CPU_CAPS=avx`) passes 434 of 435, with 22 GPU tests skipped. `guest_video_out_wqhd_detection` hit its 20 s timeout under `-j4`. Run alone it passes with this change, and it also timed out without it.

body:
### What

`addGap` and `buildEdges` each called `isZeroPadding(address, end)` at every instruction boundary. `isZeroPadding` scans from the current address to the region end, so the total work for a region with N instructions followed by a trailing-zero suffix of length Z was O(N×Z) — quadratic when Z is large.

Replace with `trailingZeroStart`, which scans backwards from the region end once to find the start of the trailing-zero suffix. The decode loop then uses that position as its stopping point, removing the per-instruction zero check entirely. The decode call itself continues to receive the original region end as the byte limit so that multi-byte instructions whose body contains zero bytes are decoded correctly.

`buildEdges` previously reset `lastFlow` to `Sequential` when the walk met zero padding, which gave a region ending in a jump or return followed by padding its fall-through edge. The reset is kept: it applies when the walk stops before `region.End`, not when the last instruction merely ends in zero bytes. `fallthroughAfterZeroPadding` in `StrictNidFilterTests.cpp` covers it and fails without the reset.

This PR no longer carries the `ElfReader.cpp` change; that stays in #1521.

### Tested

- Linux: `strict_nid_filter_tests` passed, including the new `fallthroughAfterZeroPadding` case, which fails when the reset is removed.
- Conventions check: passed (`python3 tools/check_conventions.py --base origin/main`)
- Timing (`AnalyzeStrictReachability`, one run of zero bytes followed by two `nop`s, `g++ -O2`, best of 3; first reported by @Dextroid17, re-measured here):

  | zero bytes | `main` | this PR |
  |---|---|---|
  | 25 000 | 45.6 ms | 1.0 ms |
  | 50 000 | 182.8 ms | 2.0 ms |
  | 100 000 | 718.1 ms | 4.2 ms |
  | 200 000 | 2898.7 ms | 8.8 ms |

body:
### What
On Windows, a `sceKernelRaiseException` handler that sleeps left the thread it interrupted asleep for good, if that thread was itself sleeping.

`SleepUntil`, `PollSleepUntil` and `SleepNanosCoarse` each wait on one `thread_local` high-resolution timer through `TimerWait`. When a thread is blocked in an alertable `TimedWait` wait, a raise runs the handler as an APC inside that wait (#760). If the thread was sleeping and the handler sleeps too, the handler's `TimerWait` re-arms the same timer. The handler's own wait then consumes the signal, because it is a synchronization timer. When the handler returns, the interrupted sleep waits again on a timer that will not fire, so it never returns.

`TimerWait` now counts how deep it is on the thread. A nested call creates its own timer for that wait and closes it afterwards. The outermost call keeps using the thread's timer, so nothing changes outside an APC.

I found this while testing #1476 on Windows; #1476 fixes the same reuse for `Condition` waiters. Unity's GC handler waits in `sceKernelSyncOnAddressWait`, which is #1476's case, so this one only bites a handler that sleeps. If #1476's author would rather fold this in, I'll close this PR.

The new test `guest_raise_nested_sleep` is Windows only, like `guest_raise_exception`. A thread sleeps 1 s in `sceKernelUsleep`, a raise runs a handler that sleeps 20 ms, and the 1 s sleep must return within 1 to 2 s. It has its own file, so it doesn't add to the overlapping changes in `GuestRaiseException.cpp`.

### Tested
Windows 10 (19045), MinGW-w64 GCC 15.2.0 (WinLibs r7), Release, Intel Core i7-12700H.

| Build | `guest_raise_nested_sleep` | With `APS5_COARSE_TIMED_WAITS=1` |
|---|---|---|
| `main` 4a14093a, without the fix | aborts after 5.2 s in 3 of 3 runs (the interrupted sleep has not returned) | aborts in 2 of 2 runs |
| This change | 20 of 20 pass, 1.03 s each | 3 of 3 pass |

Full ctest: 437 of 438 pass. The one failure is `agc_driver_srgb8_color_target` (#1434).

Not run on Linux. The change is inside `#ifdef _WIN32`, and the test is registered on Windows only.

### What

On Windows, `utimes` and `futimes` discarded the microsecond fields when passing timestamps to `_wutime`. The stat bridge also reported zero fractional seconds, even when the file contained a precise native timestamp. The existing filesystem test requested a half-second timestamp but checked only whole seconds.

This change:
- Sets access and modification times with `SetFileTime`, retaining guest microseconds. Null time arrays use the current Windows clock.
- Reads native access, modification, creation and metadata-change times through `FileBasicInfo`, retaining 100-nanosecond precision. `st_ctim` uses metadata change time and `st_birthtim` uses creation time.
- Uses `ReOpenFile` for regular-file descriptor updates, including read-only descriptors, so the operation targets the open file rather than reopening its pathname.
- Rejects invalid microsecond fields in the path-based API as well as the descriptor-based API, and rejects Windows timestamp conversion overflow.
- Adds the registered `guest_file_timestamps` regression test and documents the remaining host limits.

Native API behavior follows Microsoft's [SetFileTime](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-setfiletime), [FILE_BASIC_INFO](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/ns-winbase-file_basic_info), and [ReOpenFile](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-reopenfile) documentation.

### What

`wcsrtombs` passed guest strings and conversion state directly to the host CRT. On Windows, an invalid character such as U+0100 returned host `EILSEQ=42` instead of guest `86`. On Linux, the host's 32-bit `wchar_t` also disagrees with the guest's 16-bit characters.

body:
### What

Converted Linux guest libraries without `PT_GNU_STACK` can fail to load on glibc 2.41+: its absence is interpreted as an executable-stack requirement, and `dlopen` refuses it when the process stack is non-executable ([glibc change](https://sourceware.org/pipermail/glibc-cvs/2024q4/086970.html)).

Emit a default RW, non-executable stack header only when absent. Preserve explicit input headers, including executable flags and stack-size hints. The regression converts headerless, RW and RWX fixtures, verifies the output headers, and on Linux x86-64 loads the first two outputs, calls their export and verifies that the process stack remains non-executable. The original headerless input reproduces `cannot enable executable stack as shared object requires`; the fixed output loads and returns 42. The #1156 discussion encountered the same loader failure.

Rebuilt directly on `main` `d70b8998`: one commit, four files. No changes from #1265, #1913, #1986 or #1999 remain. Main's merged #1586 unwind-header constant is preserved. The stack change is independently mergeable.

### Tested

All three related tests execute on Linux and Windows; Linux x86-64 additionally performs native loading and checks process-stack permissions. Windows checks ELF conversion and headers.

### What

`sceKernelGetProcessTime` and `sceKernelGetProcessTimeCounter` computed `GetMonotonicNanos() - GetStartNanos()` in one expression. The evaluation order of the two calls is unspecified, and GCC reads the clock first. `GetStartNanos()` captures the process start on its first call, so on the first call in a process the start was taken after the clock reading and the result wrapped to about 2^64.

body:
### What

I measured `sceVideoOutInitializeOutputOptions` and `sceVideoOutIsOutputSupported` on a PS5 (firmware 13.60) by loading `libSceVideoOut.sprx` with `dlopen` from a homebrew payload. The payload opened its own handle (`sceVideoOutOpen(255, 0, 0, NULL)`), queried it, and closed it. It never called `sceVideoOutConfigureOutput`.

| Call | Console | `main` |
|---|---|---|
| `InitializeOutputOptions(&opts)` | the 64 bytes are zero except **byte 2 = `0xFF`** | all zero |
| `InitializeOutputOptions(NULL)` | `0x80290002` INVALID_ADDRESS | throws |
| `IsOutputSupported` with handle `-1`, `0`, `1`, `INT_MAX`, or a closed handle | `0x8029000B` INVALID_HANDLE, whatever the other arguments | throws |
| reserved pointer or reserved value non-zero | `0x80290001` INVALID_VALUE (checked before the mode) | throws |
| mode `1` | `1` | `1` |
| mode `15` (119.88 Hz) on a 120 Hz TV | `1` | `0` |
| modes `4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19` | `0x80290016` UNSUPPORTED_OUTPUT_MODE | `0` |
| every other value from 0 to 63, `0x100`, `0xd000000a`, `0xffffffff`, `2^63+1`, `~0` | `0x8029001E` | `0` |
| options all zero, or any bit flipped outside word 3 (mode 1) | `0x80290001` INVALID_VALUE (checked after the mode) | throws INVALID_OPTION |
| any value in word 3 (each of the 32 bits, and all of them) | accepted | throws |
| null options | accepted | accepted |

So the console never answers 0. It checks the handle, then the reserved arguments, then the mode, then the options. With this branch, `IsOutputSupported` and `ConfigureOutput`, which validates the same way, return those codes. The only answer that depends on the display is mode 15. This branch keeps the current policy of supporting only the default mode, so 15 gets UNSUPPORTED_OUTPUT_MODE, which is what [PS5_Vulkan measured](https://github.com/mihawk-99/PS5_Vulkan/blob/5b5e4fc2d80fdb67a4f61ba9e6a8a424026bb8a5/docs/HARDWARE_FINDINGS.md) `ConfigureOutput(15)` returns for a title that does not declare high-frame-rate output. Their independent mode table, from another console, agrees with mine except for mode 18: they got `0x80290016`, I got `0x8029001E`. Mode 18 therefore throws here. `0x8029001E` has no public name: the PS4 VideoOut error list ends at `0x8029001A`. I named it `VIDEO_OUT_ERROR_UNKNOWN_OUTPUT_MODE`, and the TechnicalDebt entry says the name is ours.

`VideoOutDriver::IsOpen` throws for a handle that does not exist, and other functions rely on that. So this adds `HasConfig`, which only checks whether the handle is open, and `validateOutputConfig` uses it before calling `IsOpen`.

Title: Propagation: Paradise Hotel (PPSA15878) calls `sceVideoOutInitializeOutputOptions(&opts)` and then `sceVideoOutIsOutputSupported(handle, 15, &opts, 0, 0)`. If the answer is 1, it calls `sceVideoOutConfigureOutput(handle, 15, &opts, 0, 0)` and checks its result against `0x80290016`. The first two are called from one direct call site each in the game executable. `ConfigureOutput` is called from two sites. On `main`, the title's mode 15 query returns 0, a value the console never returns. Its param.json has attribute3 `0x20c00`, without the high-frame-rate bit, so a console would not configure 15 for it either. Answering UNSUPPORTED_OUTPUT_MODE keeps it at 59.94 Hz, as on hardware.

### Tested

- PS5 firmware 13.60: every row of the table. The probe source and the raw output are in the comment below.
- Linux: build, `libs`, full CTest 431/431 (on main as of today). The new `guest_video_out_output_mode` covers every measured row; `video_out_flip_tests` (not in CTest) builds with its updated expectations.
- Windows Server 2025 VM, WinLibs GCC 15.2, CI configure flags: build, `libs`, CTest 0 failed of 407, `guest_video_out_output_mode` included (GPU execution tests skipped, the VM has no GPU).
- Mutation check: 15 mutations each make `guest_video_out_output_mode` fail. They cover the handle, reserved, and options checks, the free word, the first word, the unsupported and unknown mode sets, mode 18, the null-options path, `InitializeOutputOptions`, and `HasConfig` on a closed port. A 16th mutation (`return 1` → `mode == DEFAULT ? 1 : 0`) is equivalent, since only the default mode reaches that line.

body:
### What

Engines alias transient render targets, so a texture can sit at the address of a depth surface after that memory has been handed to a color image: a 384x384 R11G11B10 texture over a 384x384 D32S8 surface, for example. `DepthSurfaceTexture` sent every texture at a depth surface's address to `DepthSurface::Sampled`, which threw `sampling the depth plane ... is not implemented`, and the draw was skipped.

Now a view with a different extent, or a depth-plane view in a format that cannot hold the plane, is treated as reused memory. "Cannot hold the plane" means it is neither the plane's own R32F / R16 unorm nor a T# that reads the raw depth bits. The lookup returns null, so the texture goes through the ordinary texture path, as it would at any other address. Stencil-plane views keep their current handling.

#425 rewrites `DepthSurfaceTexture` for array and cube depth reads but has no reuse rule. The two touch the same function, so whichever merges second needs a small rebase.

### Tested

- PPSA16064 (Minecraft Dungeons II): the main menu's 384x384 draw that samples the reused memory (`... as a 384x384 texture of guest format 36 (vk 122), tile mode 7 ...`) was skipped every frame. It now records, and that skip no longer appears in the log.

body:
### What

`StorageTexture::FindPending` returned the first pending storage image at a texture's address that is at least as long as the surface. When transient surfaces alias, that can be the wrong image.

Unreal's depth of field does this: the reduce pass writes a 2-mip 1424x800 RGBA16F chain, and right after, the post-filter and bokeh scatter write a 1-mip 1424x800 surface at the same address, each with its own DCC keys. When the recombine sampled the newer single-mip surface, the lookup could pick the older chain. The chain's view was then refreshed under its own keys, which the title had already re-filled with a fast-clear code, so whole blocks read as the clear value (0, 0, 0, 1) instead of what the GPU had just written. On screen these were large black rectangles at 8x8-workgroup granularity, at the same positions every frame.

Now an image whose length equals the surface's wins. A longer chain still serves a descriptor of its first mips when no exact image is pending, so the containment case it was written for is unchanged.

### Tested

Windows 11, NVIDIA RTX 5070 (driver 610.88).

- PPSA16064 (Minecraft Dungeons II): the title screen's DOF recombine output had fixed black rectangles covering most of the screen. With this change the whole frame renders. I located the cause by probing the recombine's registers per pixel: in the holes, the foreground-layer sample came back as (0, 0, 0, 1) while the GPU-side image held the real data.
- `ctest`: 426 of 426 pass on current `main` with this PR and #1495 (unrelated files) applied.

### What
Every tessellated draw throws today: `DecodeShaderStages` rejects PRIMGEN_PASSTHRU_EN, the local program ends in an unresolvable `s_setpc_b64`, and hull and domain programs keep unlowered ring bases. Since #639 a title's local programs also stop registration.

- The tessellation path accepts LS, HS and an NGG passthrough ES, reads PARTITIONING and TOPOLOGY as 3-bit fields, throws on the other `VGT_TF_PARAM` bits except DISTRIBUTION_MODE, and needs HOS levels that keep [1, 63] (AMD's Sea Islands 3D register reference); 0x286-0x287 join the draw key.
- Local and domain (ES_EN = DS) programs are prepared with their stage group, not at registration. `ResolveGraphicsStagesAbi` merges the headers over one set of defaults, which used to reset the hull's LS_HS_CONFIG and TF_PARAM. A local program the hull header leaves at address 0 is prepared at its first draw.
- The local program ends at its jump into the hull half. `TessellationLowering` lowers LDS and ring addresses affine in the control point and relative index, with strides from the code; accesses outside the patch, per-patch writes not from control point 0, other relative-index uses and a non-passthrough primitive export throw.
- Hull lanes read their own saved exec bit, also from #1264's masked copies; other masks throw; factors clamp to 63.
- Quads, isolines, CCW output and domain patch-constant reads still throw. TechnicalDebt (Functional): unwritten rings, NaN inner factors, DISTRIBUTION_MODE, the local-to-hull handoff, late local programs.

body:
### What
In an address-based build, a buffer view that runs from one host-imported registered range into the next is bound past the first range's import: `UploadPrepare` merges the view into that range's region and keeps the import (`Region::direct`). `Descriptor` then returns the import's buffer with `offset + range` past its size, and `AddressRanges` maps the whole region, the next range included, through the import's device address.

- A merge that extends a region past its end now drops its import, so the region looks for an import that covers it and otherwise takes the copy path, as a range crossing an image mirror's end already does. Descriptor-only builds are unchanged.
- Like every copied range, it is read-only to pointers: a pointer store into it now takes the BDA permission fault, where `main` stored into the first range in place.
- With #1270's end check, PPSA26344 v1.008's G-buffer draws throw `guest buffer view exceeds its GPU owner` (190 skips in 3,000 s); a view across two imported ranges gives the same error, but the draws' V# comes from SRT memory and is not traced.
- #1270 (ours) adds that end check. #1345 rewrites this merge loop in place and merges cleanly; #290, #1357, #1359, #1361, #1364 and #1366 edit other parts of `UploadPrepare`.

body:
### What
On Windows, blocking audio calls paced themselves with `nanosleep` and `this_thread::sleep_for`/`sleep_until`. With MinGW these go through winpthreads, which ends a wait only on a 15.6 ms `GetTickCount64` step (#1471), so a game's audio thread ran in bursts:
- **`sceAudioOutOutput`:** a blocking output returned at once 2 times in 3 and then waited about 16 ms. This held for a device port, which re-checks the SDL queue every `DRAIN_SLEEP_US`, and for a port without a device, which sleeps in `paceVirtualPort`.
- **`sceAudioOut2ContextPush`:** a blocking push on a full queue re-checked every `FULL_WAIT_STEP`, so it returned in groups of 3 about every 16 ms.
- **`sceAudio3dPortPush`:** a blocking push slept until a frame had played. It woke up to 15.6 ms late, and frames left to play run from now once the queue has emptied. A port with 5.33 ms frames therefore took 7.8 ms per push on average, about 68 % of real time.
- **`sceAudioInInput`:** without a device it sleeps until the next block, with intervals from 0.9 ms to 31 ms instead of 16 ms. With a device, it polls the SDL queue every `sleep_for(1 ms)`.

These calls now sleep with `PreciseSleepUs`, and with a new `PreciseSleepUntil` built on it, in `libc/include/PreciseWait.hpp`. Both use a high-resolution waitable timer on Windows and `this_thread::sleep_for` elsewhere.

Overlap: #1431 makes `sleepUs` in `AudioOut.cpp` retry `nanosleep` on `EINTR`. This change removes `sleepUs`, and libstdc++'s `sleep_for`, which `PreciseSleepUs` uses on Linux, already retries on `EINTR`.

### Tested

| `sceAudioOutOutput`, device port | 5.33 ms | 187 to 188 of 300 under 1 ms, 112 to 113 over 10 ms, max 17.7 ms | 3.1 to 8.5 ms, median 5.52 to 5.56 ms |

body:
### What

Hollow Knight: Silksong (PPSA12544) ships its own `sce_module/libc.prx` and Unity's `Media/Modules/PS5Util.prx`. Both import `_umtx_op` (NID `04AjkP0jO9U`) from libkernel, which AnyPS5 does not export, so on Linux the relinked title stops at load with `undefined symbol: 04AjkP0jO9U`.

This adds `_umtx_op` to libkernel for the operations those modules pass, following FreeBSD 11's [kern_umtx.c](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/stable/11/sys/kern/kern_umtx.c):

| op | name | behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | `UMTX_OP_WAIT` | sleep while the 64-bit value at `obj` equals `val`; return 0 at once when it differs (`do_wait`, compat32 = 0) |
| 11 / 15 | `UMTX_OP_WAIT_UINT` / `_PRIVATE` | the same with a 32-bit comparison (`do_wait`, compat32 = 1) |
| 3 / 16 | `UMTX_OP_WAKE` / `_PRIVATE` | wake up to `val` waiters; `val <= 0` still wakes one (`umtxq_signal_queue`) |

Timeouts follow `umtx_copyin_umtx_time`: when `uaddr` (the size) is at most 16, `uaddr2` is a relative `timespec`; otherwise it is an `_umtx_time`, absolute with `UMTX_ABSTIME` on its clock. A negative second count or a nanosecond count outside [0, 1e9) fails with `EINVAL`, and a wait that times out fails with `ETIMEDOUT`. Errors are returned as -1 with the guest `errno` set, like the system call. A null object gives `EFAULT` (except `WAKE_PRIVATE`, which does not look up the address). Operations 0 and 1 fail with `EOPNOTSUPP` and operations above 26 with `EINVAL`, as in FreeBSD 11's `op_table`. The mutex, condition variable, rwlock, semaphore, shm and robust-list operations throw `NotImplemented`, as does a misaligned object.

Waiters use the existing `sceKernelSyncOnAddressWait` queue and `TimedWait` (no platform-specific code), so `_umtx_op` and `sceKernelSyncOnAddressWake` wake each other's waiters.

**What the title calls.** I disassembled the two modules:
- `PS5Util.prx`: a wait helper at 0x700 (`UMTX_OP_WAIT`, a `timespec` built from a microsecond timeout) and a wake helper at 0x750 (`UMTX_OP_WAKE`). The result is read through `__error`.
- `libc.prx`: helpers at 0x116b80 (`UMTX_OP_WAIT_UINT`), 0x116b90 (`UMTX_OP_WAIT`) and 0x116ba0 (`UMTX_OP_WAKE`). They are used by exported atomic-wait functions (name string `SceLibcV2AtomicWait`) and by a call_once (`SceLibcIV2Once`), which waits with **operation 1** and wakes every waiter with `UMTX_OP_WAKE(INT_MAX)`.

Two things in these modules disagree with FreeBSD and could not be checked without a console. Both are recorded in TechnicalDebt:
- libc passes the WAIT operations a pointer to a **4-byte microsecond** timeout, with size 0 (the layout of `sceKernelSyncOnAddressWait`), while PS5Util passes a `timespec`. With FreeBSD's rule, libc's 4-byte value is read as a `timespec`. The nanosecond half is then almost always out of range, so the wait returns `EINVAL` at once and libc's loop checks again. Only the untimed waits (null timeout) block.
- libc's call_once waits with operation 1, which FreeBSD 11 rejects with `EOPNOTSUPP`. The once loop then checks the flag again until it reaches the done state, so it spins instead of sleeping.

AI-assisted: the call sites were found and this change was written with Claude Code.

This PR was investigated and written by Claude Code (AI), and posted by me after review.

### Tested

Arch Linux (kernel 7.2.8), i7-8750H, GTX 1050 Ti Max-Q (NVIDIA 580.178.04), GCC 16.2.1, Release build. Each run is compared with unmodified `main` bc1fbe81 on the same machine. All runs set `APS5_WRITE_WATCH_IMPORTS=watch`; without it this NVIDIA driver creates no Vulkan device (#1289) and the GPU tests are skipped.

- `ctest -j4`: 424/424 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed (baseline 423/423, 0 skipped). The only new test is `guest_umtx_op`.
- `VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS=VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation ctest -j2 -V`: 424/424 passed. 27 `Validation Error` lines, the same as the baseline, with identical per-VUID counts.
- New test `core/libs/tests/GuestUmtxOp.cpp` (modelled on `GuestSyncOnAddress`) covers:
  - a wait returning at once when the value differs;
  - 64-bit comparison for `WAIT` and 32-bit for `WAIT_UINT`;
  - relative `timespec`, relative `_umtx_time` and absolute `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` timeouts, including one in the past;
  - rejected timeouts;
  - a wake that releases a waiter without a value change;
  - the wake count (1, then 0 waking one, then `INT_MAX`), with a waiter on another address left untouched;
  - null objects, reserved and out-of-range operations, and unimplemented operations throwing.
- Mutation check. With the test kept and the fix changed, the test failed every time:
  - fix removed: the test no longer links;
  - a wake of 0 wakes nobody: test fails;
  - `UMTX_OP_WAIT` compares 32 bits: test fails;
  - the timeout is ignored: test fails.

  The fix was then restored byte for byte and rebuilt, and `guest_umtx_op` and `guest_sync_on_address` passed.
- Windows: not tested. The change has no Windows-specific code; it uses `std::uint64_t` for the guest `u_long`.
- Silksong (PPSA12544), Linux, relinked with #846 (`--module-dir Media/Plugins`) and local throwing stubs for unrelated missing imports. On `main` the loader fails with `undefined symbol: 04AjkP0jO9U`. With this change, all modules load, the title starts, reads `/app0/Media/boot.config`, and stops at a later, unrelated gap: `sceKernelLoadStartModule with start arguments not implemented`. The log does not show whether `_umtx_op` ran before that point, so the wait and wake paths are covered only by the unit test.

body:
### What

A condition wait on a recursive mutex that the waiter has locked more than once deadlocks. `waitUntil` in `Pthread/src/Cond.cpp` cleared `_count` and `_owner`, but the condition variable unlocks the native `std::recursive_timed_mutex` only once. Every `scePthreadMutexLock` on a recursive mutex locks the native mutex again, so after N locks the waiter still holds N-1 levels during the wait. The thread that should take the mutex and signal blocks in `scePthreadMutexLock`, and the waiter never wakes (an untimed wait hangs; a timed wait times out forever).

FreeBSD libthr, which the PS5 libkernel is based on, releases the mutex completely for the wait and restores the recursion count afterwards: `_mutex_cv_unlock` / `_mutex_cv_detach` save `m_count`, set it to 0 and unlock, and `_mutex_cv_lock` / `_mutex_cv_attach` put it back ([thr_mutex.c](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/release/11.0.0/lib/libthr/thread/thr_mutex.c), [thr_cond.c](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/release/11.0.0/lib/libthr/thread/thr_cond.c) `cond_wait_kernel` / `cond_wait_user`).

The fix unlocks the remaining N-1 native levels before the wait and locks them again after it. This covers `scePthreadCondWait`, `scePthreadCondTimedwait`, `pthread_cond_wait` and `pthread_cond_timedwait`, which all go through `waitUntil`. The FreeBSD behaviour is recorded in TechnicalDebt as unverified on hardware.

`guest_cond_recursive_mutex` locks a recursive mutex twice and waits with each of the four functions while another thread locks the mutex and signals. After the wake the waiter unlocks twice and a third unlock returns `SCE_KERNEL_ERROR_EPERM`.

This PR was investigated and written by Claude Code (AI), and posted by me after review.

### Tested

Arch Linux, GCC, Release, `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`, `APS5_WRITE_WATCH_IMPORTS=watch` (Intel UHD 630 + GTX 1050 Ti).

- `guest_cond_recursive_mutex`: passes; with only the `Cond.cpp` change reverted it fails (ctest timeout, the signalling thread never gets the mutex).

> ⚠️ **Needs testing on Windows before merge.** This change was not built or run on Windows: the author has no Windows machine. Please test it on Windows (build, full ctest, and a title that exercises GC delivery) before merging.

### What

On Windows, `sceKernelRaiseException` redirects a thread that is not in an alertable `TimedWait` wait: it reads the thread's context, points it at `Aps5RedirectedEntryStub`, runs the handler and resumes the thread with `RtlRestoreContext`. That context has no `CONTEXT_XSTATE`, so only the low 128 bits of each vector register are restored. The upper halves of `ymm0`-`ymm15` come back as the handler and the delivery path left them, and anything there that runs `vzeroupper` or a VEX instruction (Zen 2 guest code compiled for AVX, the CRT's `memcpy` when it copies the `CONTEXT`) clears them. A guest thread interrupted in the middle of AVX code, for example a 32-byte copy loop, then resumes with zeroed upper lanes and writes wrong data. TechnicalDebt listed this as a known gap.

- The entry stub now also stores `ymm0`-`ymm15` in the delivery it already fills with the live registers, when the CPU and the OS enable AVX (`__builtin_cpu_supports("avx")`, which checks `XCR0`).
- The redirected entry no longer calls `RtlRestoreContext` itself: a new exit routine loads the saved `ymm0`-`ymm15` and then jumps to `RtlRestoreContext`, which restores the low halves (and any change the handler made to them through `uc_mcontext`) without touching the upper halves.
- The delivery grows by 528 bytes on the target's stack below its red zone; the existing committed-stack check covers it.
- The APC path and a raise on the calling thread are unchanged: there the handler runs inside a call, where the upper halves are not preserved by either ABI.
- The TechnicalDebt line about the YMM upper halves is removed.

This touches lines that #1421 (open) and #1431 (open) also change in `Exception.cpp`, `GuestRaiseException.cpp` and `TechnicalDebt.md`; the conflicts are textual. The change does not depend on the restore path #1421 selects (`NtContinue` today, the user-mode `iretq` restore with #1421): neither touches the upper halves, which the exit loads right before it. It also applies on top of #1421; the conflicts are textual.

This PR was investigated and written by Claude Code (AI), and posted by me after review.

### Tested

**Not built or run on Windows.** I have no Windows machine, so neither the fix nor the new test phase has been compiled with MinGW or executed. What was checked:
- Offsets by hand against the Windows SDK layout: `CONTEXT` is 1232 bytes with `Rax` at 0x78, so in `Delivery` the context starts at 16, `vectors` at 1248 and `saveVectors` at 1760; the stub runs 40 bytes below the delivery, which gives the 176/1288/1800 displacements it uses. The `static_assert`s encode these and will fail the Windows build if any is wrong.
- The stub and exit assembly assemble with GNU as on Linux (x86-64).
- Linux (Arch, GCC, Release, `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`, `APS5_WRITE_WATCH_IMPORTS=watch`): the changed code is under `_WIN32` and the test is registered on Windows only, so Linux is unaffected. Full `ctest -j4`: 423/423 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped, same as `main` (bc1fbe81). Under `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation` (`ctest -j2 -V`): 423/423 passed, 27 `Validation Error` lines, the same VUIDs and counts as `main`.

What needs to be run on Windows:
- `ctest -R ^guest_raise_exception$ --repeat until-fail:20`: the new phase loads a pattern into `ymm0`-`ymm15`, spins, gets 100 raises whose handler runs `vzeroall`, and compares the registers afterwards. It is skipped on a CPU without AVX.
- Mutation check: with this branch's `Exception.cpp` reverted to `main` (test kept), the new phase should fail (the upper lanes come back zeroed); with the fix it should pass.
- Full ctest against `main`, and a Unity title that stops threads for GC (for example the one in discussion #726).
